title: Standing up for rights
hook: Sikh groups defend the right to wear articles of faith at work, school and in the forces

segments.voice: Yesterday, North America today, and your line was neighbors. Did you learn a neighbor's name? Today, what happens when a neighbor is told they can't come in as they are. Day one thousand thirty-four.

A schoolboy in England is offered a place at a private school, on one condition: take off the turban and cut the hair, to match the uniform. His father refuses. The family takes the school to court, and loses, and appeals, and the case climbs all the way to the House of Lords, which was then the country's highest court. There the judges decide that Sikhs are protected under Britain's race relations law, and that the school's rule was unlawful discrimination. One boy, one turban, and a ruling that reached far beyond one school gate.
screen: `TAKE OFF THE TURBAN, OR NO PLACE.` → `THE FATHER REFUSES.` → `ALL THE WAY TO THE LORDS.`

segments.voice: First, what's at stake. The Rehat Maryada, the Sikh code of conduct, asks initiated Sikhs to keep the five articles of faith, among them uncut hair and the kirpan, a small sword. For a Sikh who keeps them, they're not accessories to take off for work. So when a job, a school or an army says no, the question becomes a question of rights. Second, the cases. The English case was Mandla against Dowell Lee. In Canada, a student named Gurbaj Singh Multani took his school board to the Supreme Court of Canada over wearing his kirpan, and the court ruled that a total ban was not justified. In the United States, Sikh soldiers and advocacy groups such as the Sikh Coalition pressed the army to let observant Sikhs serve with turbans and beards. Third, the wider reason. The Sikh story sets this work inside a bigger frame. Tradition says Guru Tegh Bahadur gave his life defending the freedom of Kashmiri Hindus to practice their own faith, not his. Sikhs remember him as standing up for someone else's right. Fourth, the line underneath. At Ang 141 of the Guru Granth Sahib, Guru Nanak says that taking what rightfully belongs to another is as forbidden as pork to a Muslim or beef to a Hindu. The word there is hakk, what rightly belongs to someone, and some Sikhs read the line widely: a right isn't a favor, and taking it away is taking something that isn't yours. That is today's line: rights for all. Some Sikh groups argue that a ruling won for a turban protects a headscarf, a kippah and a cross as well.
screen: `ARTICLES OF FAITH, NOT ACCESSORIES.` · `ENGLAND, CANADA, THE US ARMY.` · `GURU TEGH BAHADUR, FOR OTHERS.` · `ANG 141: ANOTHER'S RIGHT.` · then, large: `RIGHTS FOR ALL.`

segments.voice: Two minutes for someone's right. Sit, and let your back be straight but easy. Bring to mind one person whose right is being quietly squeezed. Someone talked over at work. Someone told their name is too hard to say. Someone asked to hide who they are to fit in. See them clearly. Breathe in, and feel your feet on the floor, steady. Breathe out, and ask: what one thing could I say or do for them this week? Let one answer come. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Standing up for rights. Sikh groups defend the right to wear articles of faith at work, at school and in the forces, and say those rulings protect others too. Today's word.
Your line: rights for all. Today, stand up for someone's right in one small, real way, even if it's just saying, out loud, that they should be heard. Day one thousand thirty-four.

howItsDone: Sikh advocacy groups help Sikhs who are told to remove a turban or kirpan at work, school or in the military, and often work alongside other faith groups on religious freedom.

fork.setup: you're the father. your son is offered a school place if he cuts his hair and takes off his turban. what do you do?
options: accept; it's only a uniform rule.
refuse, and take it to court.
fork.reveal: he refused, lost at first, appealed, and won in the House of Lords.

original.note: hakk, a right, what rightly belongs to someone; the word behind Guru Nanak's line at Ang 141.

trapdoor: what you thought: Sikhs fight for exceptions just for themselves.
what it means: Sikh groups defend the right to wear articles of faith, and frame it as a right for everyone.
what a scholar hears: Mandla v Dowell Lee put Sikhs under British race relations law, and Sikhs tie the work to Guru Tegh Bahadur's sacrifice for others' faith and to Ang 141 on another's right.

Legal facts to verify: Mandla v Dowell Lee (lost in the lower courts, won in the House of Lords; Sikhs held an ethnic group under the Race Relations Act); Multani (Supreme Court of Canada held a total kirpan ban unjustified). No years given on purpose.
US Army accommodation and the Sikh Coalition's role described generally; please confirm.
Guru Tegh Bahadur and the Kashmiri Pandits given as 'tradition says'.
